title: What is News?
summary: News is a report of a current event: information about something that has just happened or will happen soon, not known earlier. It can be defined as a development that has happened in the past 24 hours, not known outside, of wide interest to people and generating curiosity. John Bogart: 'When a dog bites a man, that is not news ... but if a man bites a dog, that is news.' The letters of NEWS stand for North, East, West and South: news can come from anywhere. Sources of news: newspapers, radio, television, the internet.

Information such as train timings, income tax slabs or a weather report is not news; it becomes news when news value is added (a new timetable, a change in tax rates, a sudden change in weather, floods or drought). News should give something new to the reader, viewer or listener. A perfect news item answers six questions: five Ws (When, Where, What, Why, Who) and one H (How).

Journalists judge newsworthiness by news values: timeliness (new; a newspaper covers the previous day, a weekly the previous week, a 24-hour channel every second is a deadline); impact (the tsunami affected thousands); proximity (bird flu in West Bengal matters more to us than in England); controversy (conflict, arguments: Kargil); prominence (the Prime Minister's car breaking down is news); currency (current events such as the Olympics or a SAARC meeting); oddity (unusual events, e.g. a man pulling a car with his hair); emotion (human interest stories); usefulness (weather warnings to fishermen, phone numbers of hospitals, blood donors); educational value (columns on courses and careers).

By area: international, national, regional and local news; by subject: politics, sports, economy, entertainment, crime. Hard news is serious and important (India–Pakistan talks, the Prime Minister's statement in Parliament); soft news is light or human interest (a film star's wedding, a cricketer having lunch at an orphanage).

Journalists cross-check (verify) information. Objectivity means without bias (personal, political or corporate); fairness means not taking sides and seeking the version of the person accused so the story has balance; credibility is the most important virtue of a publication, because wrong news damages reputation and corrections may be missed. News is a powerful tool, positive (voluntary service by students, news on an NGO for street children) or negative (a communal clash report can provoke communities), and it can be an instrument of development (fee concession for students).

objective: State true or false: (i) Train timings are news. (ii) News is a report of a current event.
Name the types of news by area.
International, national, regional and local news.
Match: (i) Oddity (ii) Prominence (iii) Emotion (iv) Proximity with (a) the Prime Minister's visit (b) a man pulling a car by hair (c) human interest (d) nearby events.
vsa: Distinguish between hard news and soft news with examples.
Hard news is serious and important, e.g. India–Pakistan talks; soft news is light and human interest, e.g. a film star's wedding.
What is meant by objectivity and fairness in news?
Objectivity means reporting without bias; fairness means not taking sides and giving the other party's version.
Information (train timings) is general; it becomes news when something new is added, such as a changed timetable.
What is meant by currency in news?
News is about current events of wide interest, e.g. the Olympic Games held in India.
sa: Discuss the importance of timeliness, proximity and impact in news value.

Timeliness: news must be new (previous day for a paper, every second for a news channel). Proximity: events near us matter more (bird flu in West Bengal). Impact: events affecting many people are big news (the tsunami).
Write short notes on any two news values: proximity, timeliness, impact, controversy.
Timeliness: news is new and varies by medium. Impact: the wider the effect on people, the bigger the news.
Explain the five Ws and one H of news.
When, Where, What, Why, Who and How; a news item that answers all six is complete.
Explain credibility, fairness and objectivity in news.
Cross-check facts; stay unbiased; hear both sides; credibility is the most important virtue because readers trust a paper for it.
la: Define news. Describe the main types of news.

News is a report of a current event, not known earlier and of wide interest. Types: international, national, regional, local; hard and soft; by subject such as politics, sports, economy, entertainment and crime.
Timeliness, impact, proximity, controversy, prominence, currency, oddity, emotion, usefulness and educational value, each decides whether an event is newsworthy, with examples.
Explain how news acts as a powerful tool.
News can be positive (voluntary service, NGO stories), negative (communal clash reports provoking tension) and developmental (fee concession for students); credibility and fairness are essential.
